Seif 4. Some say that mitzvot do not require intent, and some say that mitzvot require intent, etc. Even within the first view there is a dispute whether one who expressly intends not to fulfill the obligation nevertheless fulfills it. It now appears to me that there is clear proof that, according to the view that intent is unnecessary, one fulfills the mitzvah even when expressly intending not to fulfill it. A practical difference arises regarding a rabbinic mitzvah, for according to all opinions it does not require intent, and thus one would fulfill it even when intending not to do so.

The proof is from Menachot 7b, where R' Yochanan says: "This teaches that sacred vessels sanctify without awareness." What follows merely from their sanctifying without awareness? Here one could expressly intend that the contents not become sanctified, so that he could later perform kemitzah. Necessarily, when awareness is not required, even an express stipulation is ineffective, and the vessel sanctifies the contents regardless. So too, where a mitzvah does not require intent, one fulfills it even if he expressly intends, or even states, that he does not wish to fulfill it. In my humble opinion, with God's help, this is clear proof.

Regarding the difficulty raised from Arachin and Sukkah against those who maintain that if one intended to fulfill the mitzvah he nevertheless did not fulfill it, see what I wrote at length in a responsum in Tuv Taam VaDaat, first edition, siman 112, Hilchot Mezuzah, in my responsum to the community of Vizhnitz.

See Magen Avraham, seif katan 3, citing Radbaz that according to all opinions a rabbinic mitzvah does not require intent. I was uncertain, however, in light of Ran's statement in Rosh Hashanah concerning one who hears from a person who is merely practicing, that he does not fulfill the obligation. Ran writes that even according to the view that intent is not required, intending the act for a different mitzvah is worse, because an act of the same category can negate it. One must therefore determine the rule for a rabbinic mitzvah: does even such a mitzvah require intent where he intended it for another mitzvah, or is intent unnecessary for a rabbinic mitzvah even in that case?

At first glance, proof may be brought from Yoma 88a. Rav states there that Ne'ilah exempts one from Maariv, and the Gemara challenges him from a baraita teaching that after Yom Kippur one recites an abridged Shemoneh Esrei. Why not say that Rav discusses one who asks beforehand, in which case we instruct him to intend during Ne'ilah to exempt Maariv as well, and he is indeed exempt, whereas the baraita discusses one who did not intend during Ne'ilah to exempt Maariv? Such a case is no better than one who recited Maariv without intending to fulfill its obligation, who would not fulfill it according to the view that Maariv is obligatory. Certainly Ne'ilah should not exempt him when he did not intend it as Maariv.

One cannot answer that the Gemara challenges Rav according to Rav's own view in Chullin, regarding a woman who was compelled to immerse and thereby became permitted, because Rav holds that mitzvot do not require intent. Here he certainly intended his prayer as Ne'ilah. According to Ran cited above, intending the act for another mitzvah should be worse. Necessarily, the reason is that prayer is rabbinic, and regarding a rabbinic mitzvah intent is unnecessary even when one intended the act for another mitzvah.

Nor can one answer that the baraita concerns one who expressly intended not to fulfill Maariv through Ne'ilah. The baraita teaches the proper initial practice: at Shacharit one recites 7 blessings, at Ne'ilah 7 and confesses, and at Maariv an abridged Shemoneh Esrei. Had it been necessary to intend during Ne'ilah not to fulfill Maariv, the baraita should have stated that as well. Since it did not, it necessarily concerns one who had no express contrary intent. If ordinary lack of intent itself meant that he did not fulfill Maariv, the Gemara's challenge would be proper because the baraita did not advise him to intend to fulfill Maariv, while Rav could have been speaking only of one who expressly intended for Ne'ilah also to discharge Maariv. Necessarily, for a rabbinic mitzvah intent is unnecessary even when the act was intended for another mitzvah. See also my work on Orach Chayyim from the year 5599, Hilchot Tzitzit, siman 8, in my responsum to the community of Podhajce.

Rabbeinu Yonah maintains that even according to the view that mitzvot do not require intent, an obligation performed through speech certainly requires intent, because speech is not equivalent to an action. In my humble opinion, one may prove otherwise from Rashi's explanation in Menachot 2b. Rashi writes concerning "a thought evident to all" that the thought relating to offerings means verbal expression. Why did Rashi need to state this? His role there is to explain, not to issue a halachic ruling, and this point is not uniquely relevant there; it would have been more appropriate in Zevachim.

It appears that Rashi intended to resolve the following difficulty. Why do the Sages invalidate the offering? We rule that an action overrides both a prior action and a prior thought. Here the person's acts demonstrate that he is offering this particular meal-offering; why should it be invalidated by his contrary thought? Rashi therefore explains that this "thought" is verbal expression, and speech is itself considered an action, as stated elsewhere: movement of the lips constitutes an action. Thus the action of speech overrides the physical action demonstrating the opposite intent.

One might reverse the argument and say that the demonstrative physical action should override the verbal action. Yet since the 2 are equal, what makes one stronger than the other? One can equally say that the verbal action overrides the demonstrative action. Since either possibility exists, we rule stringently. Furthermore, if they are equal, cancel one against the other. What remains is the thought in the heart, which also invalidates. Even if only an undifferentiated act remained, it would be invalid here. Ordinarily, an unspecified offering is valid and a thought in the heart does not invalidate it because at least an act of offering is present. Although it is not an act that proves a particular intent, it is nevertheless an act, and the offering is therefore presumed to be for its proper purpose, while an unspoken thought does not invalidate it. Here, however, there is verbal expression for an improper purpose, and that too is an action. When action is canceled against action, it is as though no action occurred at all. An unspecified designation therefore invalidates, and certainly a contrary thought in the heart invalidates. In my humble opinion, this is Rashi's intent. It follows that Rashi holds speech to be fully equivalent to action, unlike Rabbeinu Yonah.

The halachic authorities state explicitly that even according to those who hold that intent is unnecessary, one who intends not to fulfill the obligation does not fulfill it. One may ask whether intention in the heart suffices, so that inward intent not to fulfill also prevents fulfillment, or whether thoughts in the heart have no legal force, and only if he verbally states that he intends not to fulfill does he fail to fulfill.

This may be resolved from the Yerushalmi, Shabbos, chapter R' Eliezer DeMilah, halacha 2: "A Jew may perform brit milah for a Samaritan, but a Samaritan may not perform brit milah for a Jew, because he intends it for Mount Gerizim. These are the words of R' Yudan. R' Yose said: Where have we found that brit milah requires intent? Let him continue cutting until the person's soul departs." The final phrase is difficult to understand, and Korban HaEdah's explanation is exceedingly strained.

It appears, however, that the meaning is as follows. Tosafot maintains that a non-Jew acts without specific intent. Therefore, an act whose unspecified performance is deemed for its proper purpose is valid when performed by a non-Jew, whereas an act whose unspecified performance is not deemed for its proper purpose is invalid when performed by a non-Jew. R' Yose understood R' Yudan to hold that even where an unspecified act is deemed for its proper purpose, express intent for the mitzvah is required. A Samaritan's brit milah is therefore invalid lest he intend it for Mount Gerizim. Although that intent consists only of thoughts in the heart, and thus cannot actively harm, it also cannot help. The act remains unspecified, and an unspecified act would be invalid on R' Yudan's premise.

R' Yose, however, holds that where an unspecified act is presumed to be for its proper purpose, it is valid without affirmative intent, and only express intent for an improper purpose invalidates it. In that case, thoughts in the heart have no legal force and cannot harm; only a verbal declaration would invalidate. Therefore R' Yose said: "Where have we found that brit milah requires intent?" An unspecified brit milah is presumed to be for its proper purpose. Nor can one say that the person performing it acts merely for personal benefit, for would he continue cutting until the person's soul departed? Certainly he does not intend to kill him. His purpose is to effect the halachic correction of the person, and the act is therefore presumed to be for its proper purpose. Since affirmative intent is unnecessary, even if he inwardly intends it for an improper purpose, such thoughts in the heart have no legal force.

This proves that where intent is unnecessary, an inward intention not to perform the act for its proper purpose is ineffective; only an express verbal statement has force. This is how the matter appears to me at present. Perhaps God will grant me the merit to explain it more fully at another time.
